title: When Nobody Noticed the Superstar: Rajinikanth's Lesson in Ego at the Art of Living Ashram
excerpt: India's biggest film icon spent 15 days at Sri Sri Ravi Shankar's Bengaluru ashram — and discovered that the most instructive moment of his year was being completely ignored
body:
In the annals of Indian celebrity culture, few names command the gravitational pull of Rajinikanth. The Tamil superstar — whose very presence at a film premiere can halt traffic across Chennai and whose dialogue deliveries have been elevated to something approaching liturgy — recently shared an experience that, by his own telling, left him smaller than he has ever felt. And he considers it a gift.

Speaking at the 45th anniversary celebrations of the Art of Living Foundation at its sprawling international centre on the outskirts of Bengaluru, the 75-year-old actor recounted an encounter that reads like a parable about the limits of earthly fame. During a 15-day retreat at the ashram — his longest sustained spiritual immersion in recent memory — Rajinikanth found himself seated on stage during a massive public darshan attended by thousands. As the crowd swelled, the man accustomed to stadiums erupting at his silhouette tried his usual move: he waved.

"Nobody even looked at me," he recalled, a note of genuine wonder in his voice. "I was waving, but no one saw me. My ego was crushed — completely destroyed."

## A Superstar in the Crowd

The occasion was no ordinary gathering. The Art of Living's 45th anniversary, which runs from May 10 to 26 this year, coincides with founder Sri Sri Ravi Shankar's 70th birthday and has drawn delegates from 182 countries. Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the celebrations, unveiling the new Dhyan Mandir — a meditation hall — and launching nine service initiatives spanning mental health, prison reform, and education. Against this canvas of global spiritual ambition, Rajinikanth was simply another devotee.

That, he insists, was the point. The crowd's eyes were fixed on Sri Sri Ravi Shankar. No one cared that the man in the next seat had a filmography grossing thousands of crores. In the economy of the ashram, spiritual presence outranked box-office clout — and the superstar found this not insulting, but liberating.

## The Wellness Turn

For millions of Indians in the diaspora, Rajinikanth's candid admission carries particular resonance. The Art of Living Foundation operates in more than 180 countries, with chapters across the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia that serve as both spiritual anchors and community gathering spaces for NRIs. Its Sudarshan Kriya breathing technique has been adopted by corporate wellness programmes from Silicon Valley to the City of London. When a figure of Rajinikanth's stature endorses not the organisation's brand but its fundamental premise — that there is something beyond individual identity worth surrendering to — it legitimises a conversation that many in the diaspora navigate quietly.

For the generation of NRIs who grew up watching Rajinikanth defy physics on screen, his pivot toward public vulnerability marks a cultural shift. Indian masculinity, particularly as projected through cinema, has traditionally left little room for admitted fragility. The superstar who flips sunglasses and catches bullets with his bare hands is now saying, with evident relief, that being ignored was the most instructive experience of his recent life.

## Beyond the Ashram

Rajinikanth's spiritual leanings are not new. He has spoken publicly about practising meditation since the 1990s, has visited ashrams across India, and has a well-documented habit of touching the feet of spiritual leaders — whether at Sri Sri Ravi Shankar's events or during visits with other gurus. What is new is the directness and self-deprecating humour with which he now shares these experiences, suggesting not a posed spiritual brand-building exercise, but something closer to genuine integration.

The timing is notable. Rajinikanth is currently preparing for the release of *Jailer 2*, slated for August 2026, which will see him return to the commercial machinery that defines his public life. The juxtaposition is distinctly Indian: the same person can, without contradiction, promote a blockbuster action franchise and describe the dissolution of ego as his greatest recent achievement. In a culture that has historically seen no tension between material engagement and spiritual seeking — the Bhagavad Gita, after all, was delivered on a battlefield — this duality is not hypocrisy. It is tradition.

## What Stays

The Art of Living's Bengaluru campus, spread across 65 acres near the Kanakapura Road, continues its celebrations through month's end with workshops, cultural programmes, and meditation sessions open to the public. For NRIs planning summer visits to India, the event offers an unusually accessible entry point into organised spiritual practice — one now carrying the unlikely endorsement of a man whose fan clubs have their own political parties.

Rajinikanth, for his part, seems unbothered by the paradox. "The rarest thing in this world is a human life," he told the gathered crowd, quoting a teaching from his retreat. "And we waste it on ego." From anyone else, this might sound like a greeting-card platitude. From the most recognisable face in South Indian cinema, standing in an ashram where no one recognised him, it lands differently.
